lead: Every two-port parameter set is the same pair of linear equations written in a different order. Z, Y, h, g and ABCD each choose different independent and dependent variables, so one matrix follows from another by algebra. This matters when a device data sheet gives h parameters but a cascade calculation needs ABCD, or when a measured Z matrix must be checked against a Y matrix. The conversion is exact when the denominator parameter is nonzero; if it is zero, that route does not exist.
prereq: You need: Z and Y parameters, h and g parameters, ABCD parameters, plus matrix algebra and determinants.

sections.h3: One network, five ways to write it

blocks.text: A linear two-port has only two independent equations. Each parameter set chooses a different pair of variables to put on the right side. The physics does not change; only the algebra changes.
V<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>11</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>12</sub> I<sub>2</sub>; V<sub>2</sub> = z<sub>21</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>22</sub> I<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: V<sub>1</sub>, V<sub>2</sub> are port voltages in volts; I<sub>1</sub>, I<sub>2</sub> are port currents in amperes; z<sub>11</sub>, z<sub>12</sub>, z<sub>21</sub>, z<sub>22</sub> are Z parameters in ohms.

blocks.text: I<sub>1</sub> = y<sub>11</sub> V<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>12</sub> V<sub>2</sub>; I<sub>2</sub> = y<sub>21</sub> V<sub>1</sub> + y<sub>22</sub> V<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: y parameters are admittances in siemens (S); the same V and I symbols apply.

blocks.text: V<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>11</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + h<sub>12</sub> V<sub>2</sub>; I<sub>2</sub> = h<sub>21</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + h<sub>22</sub> V<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: h<sub>11</sub> is in ohms, h<sub>22</sub> in siemens, h<sub>12</sub> and h<sub>21</sub> are dimensionless.

blocks.text: I<sub>1</sub> = g<sub>11</sub> V<sub>1</sub> + g<sub>12</sub> I<sub>2</sub>; V<sub>2</sub> = g<sub>21</sub> V<sub>1</sub> + g<sub>22</sub> I<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: g<sub>11</sub> is in siemens, g<sub>22</sub> in ohms, g<sub>12</sub> and g<sub>21</sub> are dimensionless.

blocks.text: V<sub>1</sub> = A V<sub>2</sub> − B I<sub>2</sub>; I<sub>1</sub> = C V<sub>2</sub> − D I<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: A and D are dimensionless, B is in ohms, C is in siemens; I<sub>2</sub> is the current entering port 2.

blocks.text: The determinants measure coupling: Δz = z<sub>11</sub>z<sub>22</sub> − z<sub>12</sub>z<sub>21</sub> (Ω²), Δy = y<sub>11</sub>y<sub>22</sub> − y<sub>12</sub>y<sub>21</sub> (S²), Δh = h<sub>11</sub>h<sub>22</sub> − h<sub>12</sub>h<sub>21</sub> (dimensionless), Δg = g<sub>11</sub>g<sub>22</sub> − g<sub>12</sub>g<sub>21</sub> (dimensionless).

Any two sets are linked by solving one pair of equations for the other pair. A matrix inverse works only when the determinant is nonzero; a conversion formula may fail earlier when its divisor is zero.
ABCD is the common target because cascade multiplies ABCD matrices, as shown in interconnection of two-ports.

items: From V<sub>2</sub> = z<sub>21</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>22</sub> I<sub>2</sub>, solve I<sub>1</sub> = (V<sub>2</sub> − z<sub>22</sub> I<sub>2</sub>)/z<sub>21</sub>.

Substitute in V<sub>1</sub> = z<sub>11</sub> I<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>12</sub> I<sub>2</sub>. Collect V<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> to get V<sub>1</sub> = (z<sub>11</sub>/z<sub>21</sub>)V<sub>2</sub> − (Δz/z<sub>21</sub>)I<sub>2</sub>, so A = z<sub>11</sub>/z<sub>21</sub> and B = Δz/z<sub>21</sub>.
The solved I<sub>1</sub> is I<sub>1</sub> = (1/z<sub>21</sub>)V<sub>2</sub> − (z<sub>22</sub>/z<sub>21</sub>)I<sub>2</sub>, so C = 1/z<sub>21</sub> and D = z<sub>22</sub>/z<sub>21</sub>.

blocks.text: The Y and h rows come from the same substitution; the divisor y<sub>21</sub> or h<sub>21</sub> appears because that parameter multiplies the controlling variable. Some syllabi call this interrelationships among parameter sets.
Reverse conversions are obtained by solving the same equations; for example, ABCD→Z gives z<sub>11</sub>=A/C, z<sub>12</sub>=(AD−BC)/C, z<sub>21</sub>=1/C, z<sub>22</sub>=D/C.

The table fails when z<sub>21</sub>=0, y<sub>21</sub>=0, h<sub>21</sub>=0 or g<sub>21</sub>=0. Such a two-port is unilateral in the forward direction; no table route gives a finite ABCD matrix. Keep the original equations, or use another set only to represent the network for analysis.
Check units after every conversion: A and D dimensionless, B in ohms, C in siemens. A result with B in siemens means a row or column was swapped.

Use a reciprocal network as a quick check: z<sub>12</sub>=z<sub>21</sub> makes AD−BC=1. For a symmetric network z<sub>11</sub>=z<sub>22</sub>, so A=D in ABCD. These two tests catch most table look-up errors.
The h→g conversion is the matrix inverse of h: g<sub>11</sub>=h<sub>22</sub>/Δh, g<sub>12</sub>=−h<sub>12</sub>/Δh, g<sub>21</sub>=−h<sub>21</sub>/Δh, g<sub>22</sub>=h<sub>11</sub>/Δh.
A numerical check: compute one port voltage from both sets for the same I<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> and compare. If the values differ, the algebra or sign convention is wrong.
If a denominator is zero, do not force a conversion. Keep the parameter set that exists, or use the defining equations directly. The conversion is exact, not approximate.

figure.caption: The graph links the five parameter sets; each arrow is an algebraic rearrangement, and the divisor on the arrow must be nonzero.

spec.aria: A graph connects Z, Y, h, g and ABCD; each edge is a conversion step labelled with its divisor.

examples.question: A two-port has z<sub>11</sub> = 6 Ω, z<sub>12</sub> = 4 Ω, z<sub>21</sub> = 4 Ω, z<sub>22</sub> = 7 Ω. Find its ABCD matrix.
steps: The Z parameters are z<sub>11</sub> = 6 Ω, z<sub>12</sub> = 4 Ω, z<sub>21</sub> = 4 Ω, z<sub>22</sub> = 7 Ω. The conversion uses z<sub>21</sub> = 4 Ω, which is not zero.
Compute Δz = z<sub>11</sub> z<sub>22</sub> − z<sub>12</sub> z<sub>21</sub> = (6)(7) − (4)(4) = 42 − 16 = 26 Ω².
examples.answer: The ABCD matrix is A = 1.5, B = 6.5 Ω, C = 0.25 S and D = 1.75.
examples.check:
z11 = 6.0
z12 = 4.0
z21 = 4.0
z22 = 7.0
delta_z = z11 * z22 - z12 * z21
A = z11 / z21
B = delta_z / z21
C = 1 / z21
D = z22 / z21
print(A)
print(B)
print(C)
print(D)

traps: z<sub>21</sub>, y<sub>21</sub>, h<sub>21</sub> or g<sub>21</sub> in the denominator: if that parameter is zero, the conversion does not exist. A unilateral two-port often has one of these zeros.
Y = Z⁻¹ is a matrix inverse, not y<sub>11</sub> = 1/z<sub>11</sub> and y<sub>22</sub> = 1/z<sub>22</sub>. The off-diagonal terms enter through Δz.

Keep the ABCD sign convention: V<sub>1</sub> = A V<sub>2</sub> − B I<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>1</sub> = C V<sub>2</sub> − D I<sub>2</sub>. Dropping a minus sign swaps B or C and breaks cascade multiplication.
Carry units: A and D dimensionless, B Ω, C S, Δz Ω², Δy S². Δh and Δg are dimensionless.

quiz.q: Define Δz and state its unit for a two-port whose Z parameters are in ohms.
quiz.a: Δz = z<sub>11</sub>z<sub>22</sub> − z<sub>12</sub>z<sub>21</sub>; its unit is Ω².

quiz.q: Why can the same two-port be represented by Z, Y, h, g and ABCD without changing its behaviour?
quiz.a: Each set is a different choice of independent variables in the same two linear equations. Solving one pair for another gives the other set, so the port behaviour is unchanged.

quiz.q: A two-port has z<sub>11</sub>=10 Ω, z<sub>12</sub>=2 Ω, z<sub>21</sub>=5 Ω, z<sub>22</sub>=8 Ω. Find A, B, C and D.
A two-port has z<sub>21</sub>=0. Which conversion in the table cannot be used, and what does that mean physically?
quiz.a: No conversion to ABCD from the table works for this network. With z<sub>21</sub>=0, the other sets (when they exist) also have y<sub>21</sub>=h<sub>21</sub>=g<sub>21</sub>=0, so every ABCD row divides by zero. Keep the defining equations; use another parameter set only to represent the network for analysis, not to obtain ABCD. Physically, input current does not produce an open-circuit output voltage through z<sub>21</sub>.

quiz.q: For h<sub>11</sub>=1 kΩ, h<sub>12</sub>=0.001, h<sub>21</sub>=50, h<sub>22</sub>=20 μS, find A and B of the ABCD matrix.
A student converts Z to Y by taking y<sub>11</sub>=1/z<sub>11</sub> and y<sub>22</sub>=1/z<sub>22</sub>. Is that correct? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Y is the inverse of the Z matrix; the off-diagonal terms mix. For a reciprocal two-port, y<sub>11</sub>=z<sub>22</sub>/Δz, y<sub>12</sub>=−z<sub>12</sub>/Δz, y<sub>21</sub>=−z<sub>21</sub>/Δz, y<sub>22</sub>=z<sub>11</sub>/Δz.

beyond: Not for the exam. In radio-frequency work, S-parameters are measured at 50 Ω and converted to ABCD for cascading filters and amplifiers. Power-system and transformer models often use ABCD because cascade multiplication is simple. Search 'S-parameter to ABCD conversion' and 'two-port parameter conversion' to see the same algebra with complex numbers.
